14133-david-balfour-being-memoirs-of-his:
Robert Louis Stevenson's David Balfour continues the hero's story after Kidnapped, now tangled in the Appin murder case. David faces Lord Advocate Grant, suffers captivity on the Bass Rock, and travels into Holland and France. James More Drummond, son of Rob Roy, and his daughter Catriona shape the second half, with loyalty, law, and love pulling David in turn.

Stevenson warns in his dedication that sequels disappoint, then proves himself wrong. Scots speech, sea cabins, and courtroom pressure give the tale texture, while Catriona's plea for David's life on her knees forms its emotional peak. Six passengers share a cabin on one voyage, merchants from Leith, Kirkcaldy, and Dundee among them. Adventure and feeling balance here, and the novel closes David's youth with honor intact and affection earned.
21337-that-very-mab:
May Kendall and Andrew Lang wrote this satirical fantasy together, published in London in 1885, in which Queen Mab returns to modern earth. Moonlight floods a sacred island in Samoa as her voice rises from the Calling Place and the sea itself shudders. From the Pacific she comes to inspect Victorian England.

Chapters send Mab through disillusions. She meets debates on the origin of religion, a poet facing a palaeontologist of theology, machinery, the successful merchant, and justice under the new democracy. A nihilist, a democrat, and a professor offer suggestions to a bishop. The result is a light, sharp fable using fairy machinery to mock the science, politics, and sermons of 1885.
25021-battle-of-the-monkey-the-crab:
This Japanese fairy tale, number three in the Japanese Fairy Tale Series from Griffith, Farran of London and Kobunsha of Tokyo, tells the battle of the monkey and the crab. Meeting round a mountain, the monkey trades a persimmon-seed for the crab's toasted rice-cake, and the crab plants the seed. At once it springs up into a tall tree full of persimmons, which the crab cannot climb.

The monkey climbs instead, eats the ripe fruit himself, pockets the good ones, and throws the unripe ones down at the crab, bruising his shell until he escapes into his hole. The crab's relatives declare war, but the monkey's numerous following defies them, and the crabs retreat to a council of war. A rice-mortar, a pounder, a bee, and an egg then devise a deep-laid plot, beginning with a request for peace. The tale is short, sharp, and just.
25757-scarabs-the-history-manufacture-an:
Isaac Myer, member of the American Oriental Society and American Numismatic and Archaeological Society, writes this study of scarabs, their history, manufacture, and religious symbolism in ancient Egypt, Phoenicia, Sardinia, and Etruria. A transcriber note warns Myer uses commas and asterisks in unusual ways.

Myer adds remarks on learning, philosophy, arts, ethics, psychology, and ideas of immortality among ancient Egyptians and Phoenicians. Greek words appear transliterated between plus marks, and macron vowels are marked. The scarab, a beetle sacred to Egypt, becomes a window on ancient faith, craft, and trade.
27466-el-kab:
J. E. Quibell wrote this excavation report for the Egyptian Research Account of 1897, published in London by Bernard Quaritch in 1898, in association with the work of Somers Clarke and J. J. Tylor. It records the digging at El Kab, an ancient Egyptian site, with sections on the course of work, the chance of inscribed tombs, and a description of the site itself.

Chapters take up the earliest tombs, with mastabas and stairway tombs, and the dating of the New Race remains. They go on to the Middle Kingdom cemetery with early Twelfth Dynasty tombs and beads, and New Empire monuments of the Eighteenth Dynasty. The report is technical and detailed, with the measurements and finds of a working dig. Egyptology readers will find a primary source here.
4223-the-mystery-of-a-hansom-cab:
Fergus Hume's Mystery of a Hansom Cab, the best-selling Melbourne detective tale, opens its eighth chapter with Brian taking a walk and a drive. In a drawing room, a young lady plays a detestable morceau de salon, variations embroidering an air till the tune is an agony to find.

The melody is Over the Garden Wall, with variations by Signor Thump, a comic touch in a murder mystery. Hume builds his plot from cab rides, society parties, and a dead man found in a cab. Readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction will find a fast, atmospheric puzzle.
britannica-1911-ab: Ab is the headword of a short calendar entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names the fifth month of the church year and the eleventh of the civil year of the Jews, falling near mid-July to mid-August. The name came from Babylon, taken up after the exile. Tradition sets Aaron's death on its first day. Its ninth day holds the Fast of Ab, kept in grief for the first temple, lost to Nebuchadrezzar, and the second, lost to Titus.
britannica-1911-ahab:
Ahab, king of Israel, is treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son and successor of Omri, he came to the throne about 875 B.C. His marriage to Jezebel, daughter of the king of Sidon, tied Israel to Phoenician trade. Great riches followed, bringing pomp and luxury, an ivory palace, and newly founded cities.

That same marriage drove the reign's religious conflict. Jezebel held fast to the Tyrian Baal, Melkart, and Ahab built Baal a temple in Samaria. Prophets seeking to purify the worship of Yahweh, Elijah among them, rose in anger. Moab stayed tributary, while war with Damascus brought a lenient settlement that a popular story condemned. Three years later Ahab was mortally wounded fighting beside Jehoshaphat of Judah to recover Ramoth-Gilead.
britannica-1911-aintab:
Aintab, ancient Doliche, a town in the vilayet of Aleppo in northern Syria, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Two thirds of its 45,000 people were Moslem. The old site of Doliche, famous for worship of Baal as Zeus Dolichenus, lies at Duluk nearby, where little shows but a mound. The town itself was probably of Hittite origin.

Aintab's bazaars formed a great centre for Hittite antiquities dug up across the region. The modern town stands in an open, treeless valley on the Sajur river, on the highway between northern Syria and Urfa and Mosul, with much transit trade and many khans. Lying high, at 3,500 feet, and swept by purifying winds, it was fairly clean and healthy. The American Mission Board made it a centre, with Central Turkey College for education and medicine on high ground west of town.
britannica-1911-chenab:
Chenab is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on one of the “Five Rivers” of the Punjab in India, the Greek Acesines. It rises in the snowy Himalayan ranges of Kashmir. It enters British territory in the Sialkot district and flows through the Punjab plains. On its way it forms the boundary between the Rechna and Jech Doabs. At last it joins the Jhelum at Trimmu.

The entry adds the work the river made possible. The Chenab Canal, opened in 1887, is called the largest and most profitable perennial canal in India. It watered the desert of the Bar. The Chenab Colony was formed in 1892 from parts of three districts to settle that watered land. It held 791,861 people in 1901, and its planned irrigated area was two and a half million acres. Its principal town is Lyallpur, named for a lieutenant governor of the Punjab.
britannica-1911-crab:
Crab is a name given to the crustacea of the order Brachyura. It also covers other forms, above all of the order Anomura, that match them in look and habits. True crabs split from the long-tailed lobsters and shrimps of the order Macrura in one plain way. Their abdomen, or tail, is small in size. It is carried folded up under the body.

In most kinds the body takes a broad oval or triangular outline, more or less flattened. A hard shell, the carapace, covers the whole frame. The first pair ends in nippers and is far more massive than the rest. The other legs serve for walking or swimming. Eyes sit on movable stalks and can draw back into sockets. Six pairs of jaws and foot-jaws sit in a mouth cavern. The abdomen is narrow and triangular in males, but broad and round in females.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achab:
Achab, son of Amri and King of Israel, reigned 918 to 897 BC by 1 Kings 16:29, though Assyrian documents give 875 to 854, and the original reading may have changed. Married to Jezabel, a Sidonian princess, he was misled by her into idolatry, persecution of the prophets, and grievous injustice against Naboth. He twice defeated Syria in war, then allied with the Syrian king Benadad despite prophetic warning.

In Salmanassar II's sixth year the allies were beaten near Karkar by the Assyrians, ending their compact. Achab then allied with Josaphat of Juda to conquer Ramoth Galaad. False prophets promised victory; Micheas predicted defeat. An arrow wounded Achab between lungs and stomach, he died that evening, and dogs licked his blood where his chariot was washed in Samaria's pool.
doe-osti-2999077-sceptre-a-cyber-physica: Hacking a fake power grid got its DOE playground, and this text builds the SCEPTRE emulator. The pages detail the virtual hardware. The security researchers get their tool. The playground was cyber-physical. The hardware was virtual. The emulator was SCEPTRE.
doe-osti-3002212-assessment-of-minifcci-: A tiny reactor test rig got its DOE checkup, and this text sizes up what MiniFCCI can take. The pages detail the capability. The reactor crew gets its data. The rig was MiniFCCI. The data were crew's. The checkup was DOE's.
doe-osti-3025871-ai-ready-control-system: Fermilab accelerators got AI-readied, and this DOE text controls the complex. The pages detail the system findings. The physicists get their data. The system was control. The data were physicist. The complex were accelerator. The ready were AI. The Fermilab were complex.
doe-osti-3369031-phenomena-identificatio: PIRT got blade-erosion-ranked, and this DOE analysis covers wind turbines. The pages detail the phenomena findings. The energy folks get their data. The erosion was leading edge. The data were energy. The PIRT were tables. The edge were leading.
doe-osti-3375394-complete-time-resolved-: MRT 8818 got X-ray-shaped, and this DOE milestone covers 10 MJ implosions. The pages detail the complete findings. The physicists get their data. The capability was time-resolved. The data were physicist. The 8818 were MRT. The implosion were MJ. The resolved were time.
doe-osti-3394710-phenomena-identificatio: PIRT got microreactor-ranked, and this DOE tables cover gas-cooled reactors. The pages detail the phenomena findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The temperature was high. The data were nuclear. The microreactors were tables. The gas-cooled were reactors.
doe-osti-3677342-final-technical-report-: When hurricanes knock out the grid, the poorest neighborhoods wait longest for power. The REDDI Communities final report covers resilient renewable energy projects that shrink disaster impact. Solar-plus-storage systems keep clinics, shelters, and homes running when the grid fails.
nasa-tm-19650014229-some-design-consider:
Robert H Johns, Reeves P Cochran, and David A Spera at Lewis Research Center wrote this report on spinning satellites with expandable structures. Some spacecraft need large flat areas, for radiators, solar collectors, or dust-catching experiments. Those areas must unfold or expand after launch, since a rocket nose cone is small.

Spinning keeps such a satellite steady, but it also stresses the expanded parts. The authors weigh design choices for that combination. They look at rigid expandable structures, which hold their shape once opened. The problem is a balance: enough area for the job, enough strength to survive spin, and a package small enough to launch.
nasa-tm-19690010288-a-systems-analysis-o:
A systems analysis of a regenerative cabin atmosphere control system forms this master's thesis in mechanical engineering. It comes from the University of Virginia's School of Engineering and Applied Science. Regenerative systems recycle cabin air for long missions instead of storing all breathing gases at launch. The thesis first models a space cabin, its crew, and its atmosphere.

Long chapters then describe each component in turn. They include blowers and ducting, water separators, bypass dampers, and a carbon dioxide concentrator. A reduction unit and an electrolysis unit follow, with nitrogen control and pressure sensors after them. System block diagrams then tie the parts together. The whole forms an engineering blueprint for keeping cabin air breathable on long flights.
the-mystery-of-a-hansom-cab:
Fergus Hume's detective novel The Mystery of a Hansom Cab is present here only through a full contents list. A bare heading, Preface, follows it. Neither the preface text nor the story appears. Thirty-five chapters are listed. What the Argus Said opens the book, and The Evidence at the Inquest follows, with a hundred pounds reward offered in Chapter III.

A detective named Gorby makes a start and further discoveries, while another investigator, Kilsip, later forms a theory of his own. The Trial, The Verdict of the Jury, and Sal Rawlins Tells All She Knows fill the middle list. Hush-Money, The Confession, and The Hands of Justice close the visible contents near the end.
